title: GPT-6.1 Terra vs Sol and Kimi K3.1 Pro: which model offers better value?
description: Terra lowers the cost of capable computer-use agents, while Sol and Kimi retain higher ceilings. Independent tests show where each model fits.

sections.heading: Terra changes the workhorse tier rather than the capability ceiling
paragraphs: OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Terra is a consequential release because it places a capable visual and computer-use model between the budget GPT-6 Luna tier and the stronger GPT-6.1 Sol. Standard API pricing is $1 per million input tokens, $0.05 per million cached input tokens, and $5 per million output tokens. That is half Sol's $2/$10 rate and below the previous GPT-5.6 Terra's $2/$12. The official API documentation confirms a 1.05-million-token context window, 128,000 maximum output tokens, text and image input, computer use, and six reasoning settings from none through max.

Independent Artificial Analysis testing scores Terra at 48 on Intelligence Index v4.3.2 at maximum effort, four points below GPT-6.1 Sol. The evaluator measured about $0.40 per Intelligence Index task, compared with $0.72 for Sol, and found Terra's low and medium settings on the cost-efficiency frontier. The useful conclusion is not that Terra universally replaces Sol. It is that teams can now buy much of Sol's measured capability for a lower task cost when visual understanding, desktop interaction, and routine professional work dominate the queue.

OpenAI reports that Terra approaches Astra and Sol on visual reasoning and computer use while finishing tasks more than three times faster in its tests. Those speed, task-cost, factuality, and benchmark comparisons are vendor-reported. They identify promising workloads, but they do not establish the result for a private application, network region, tool harness, or review standard. Artificial Analysis independently supports the broader cost-efficiency case, while still showing a material capability gap on harder general and coding tasks.

sections.heading: Sol remains the control when difficult coding and completeness matter
paragraphs: GPT-6.1 Sol remains the stronger OpenAI default for tasks where a failed attempt costs more than the model call. Artificial Analysis scores Sol at 52 on the same Intelligence Index, versus Terra's 48, and at 54 on Coding Agent Index v2.0, versus Terra's 48. Terra made a roughly twenty-point jump over its predecessor on Terminal-Bench 4.0 and now rivals Sol at maximum effort there, but one terminal benchmark does not erase Sol's broader advantage across the index.

The practical boundary is verification cost. Terra is the better first route for invoice and form workflows, visual document processing, application-screen interaction, routine coding, and professional drafting when tests or checklists expose failure cheaply. Sol deserves the first attempt for ambiguous repository work, harder multi-step agents, and deliverables where omissions are expensive to find. Since both models support multiple effort settings, compare Terra at low and medium with the existing Sol setting before comparing only their maximum configurations.

Long context complicates both price cards. OpenAI charges two times the input and cache rates and one and a half times the output rate for an entire request above 272,000 input tokens. Terra's low headline price therefore does not justify sending every repository or document archive in one prompt. Retrieval, compaction, and cache reuse remain important. Tool calling also requires the Responses API, so a migration from another endpoint should be treated as an integration test rather than only a model-name substitution.

sections.heading: Kimi K3.1 Pro buys a higher agent ceiling, but not open weights yet
paragraphs: Moonshot's Kimi K3.1 Pro creates a different value proposition. Its official API price is $2 per million input tokens, $0.20 for cached input, and $10 per million output tokens—the same uncached rate as Sol and one third below Kimi K3. It supports text and image input across a 1,048,576-token window, always uses reasoning, and offers low, high, and max effort. Moonshot describes it as a heavily post-trained 2.8-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts model with 104 billion active parameters.

Artificial Analysis scores K3.1 Pro at 55, three points above Sol and seven above Terra on the current Intelligence Index. It also reports 67% on Terminal-Bench 4.0, the highest result in that evaluation at publication, plus strong professional knowledge-work and automation results. The trade-off is consumption: the evaluator measured about 55,000 output tokens and $1.98 per Intelligence Index task. K3.1 Pro therefore offers the highest measured capability of this group, but Terra and Sol can be cheaper routes even when their posted token rates do not tell the whole story.

K3.1 Pro should not yet be described as open weight. Moonshot says full weights will be released by November 4, but they are not currently published with a downloadable checkpoint and license. Until that happens, K3 remains Moonshot's self-hostable catalog option and K3.1 Pro is an API model with a promised future release. Its official guide also says thinking cannot be disabled and its web-search tool is being updated and is not recommended for production, two operational limits that belong in any migration test.

sections.heading: Route by failure cost, then measure the whole accepted task
paragraphs: A minimal evaluation needs twenty to fifty completed tasks drawn from the intended workload. Include application screens, image-heavy documents, repository changes, tool failures, long inputs, and deliverables that previously needed human correction. Run Terra at low and medium, the current Sol configuration, and K3.1 Pro at low or high when its stronger agent performance could matter. Record accepted completion, omitted requirements, reviewer minutes, retries, input and cached tokens, output tokens, latency, tool calls, safety interruptions, and final billed cost.

The first routing policy should stay deliberately small. Use Terra for high-volume visual work, computer use, routine coding, and writing with cheap verification. Keep Sol for difficult coding and structured agents where its higher independent scores reduce failures. Pilot K3.1 Pro for long-horizon terminal, 3D, financial-research, and professional-work tasks that can justify its higher measured cost. Do not plan a self-hosted K3.1 deployment until the promised weights and license can be inspected directly.

Safety and authorization checks remain part of capability testing. OpenAI's system card classifies Terra as Critical in cybersecurity and applies the Astra safeguard stack, but it also reports higher unauthorized-action rates than Sol in one adversarial external-agent-message evaluation. That is vendor-run safety evidence, not a production incident rate. It is still a reason to require confirmation for irreversible actions and to verify final state rather than trusting a fluent completion. The durable buying rule is simple: Terra is the new cost-efficient workhorse, Sol is the stronger OpenAI control, and K3.1 Pro is the higher-scoring agent candidate whose open-weight promise remains unfulfilled until the files actually ship.
bullets: Cost-efficient workhorse: GPT-6.1 Terra at low or medium effort for visual and computer-use workflows.
Stronger OpenAI control: GPT-6.1 Sol for difficult coding and higher-cost failures.
Highest measured ceiling in this group: Kimi K3.1 Pro, currently API-only despite promised weights.
Vendor-reported: launch speed, factuality, and model-card benchmark claims; independently measured: Artificial Analysis intelligence, coding, token-use, and task-cost results.

title: Gemini 4 Carbon vs Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra: wait or switch?
description: Carbon leads the new independent intelligence index, but restricted access and heavy token use make Argon, Opus, and Astra the practical controls.

sections.heading: Carbon is the new measured leader, not yet a production default
paragraphs: Google announced Gemini 4 Carbon on October 28, only two weeks after making Gemini 4 Argon broadly available. Carbon is a genuine frontier upgrade rather than a renamed endpoint. Artificial Analysis scores its high-reasoning configuration at 59 on Intelligence Index v5, first among the models tested under the new benchmark mix. It also scores 59 on the evaluator's Coding Agent Index, three points behind Claude Opus 5.5 at maximum effort. Those independent results make Carbon a serious future buying candidate.

Availability prevents an immediate migration. Google is initially giving access to selected cyber defenders and trusted partners through its Fairwind Program while it gathers feedback and refines safeguards. The company says developer, business, and consumer access will follow, but it has not published a date or a general API model identifier. Artificial Analysis likewise notes that Carbon is not publicly available. A model that a small evaluation cohort can test is not yet interchangeable with Opus, Astra, or Argon in a production architecture.

The price also needs a date attached. Google announces introductory rates of $2 per million input tokens, $10 per million output tokens, and a 95% cached-input discount. Standard pricing will be $4/$20, but Google has not named the introductory period's end. Artificial Analysis therefore uses the standard rate in its cost comparisons. Procurement models should do the same until the discount deadline and general-access terms are documented.

sections.heading: Independent results show a broad leap with expensive verbosity
paragraphs: Carbon leads four of the nine components in Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5: HLE-Diamond, Terminal-Bench-Science, AA-Omniscience, and AutomationBench-AA. Its 59-point composite result is nine points above Argon under the evaluator's current methodology. On coding agents, Carbon reaches 64% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 and 51% on FrontierCode v1.1, placing second to Opus 5.5 in both. This is stronger evidence than a vendor launch table because one evaluator ran the compared models through a common framework.

It is not a clean sweep. Carbon's 1,609 Elo on AA-Briefcase improves sharply over Argon, but still trails Kimi K3.1 Pro, Muse Wonder, and Grok 4.7 on that agentic knowledge-work evaluation. Artificial Analysis also measured about 123,000 output tokens per Intelligence Index task. At standard $4/$20 pricing, the resulting $7.76 average task cost is about 23% below Opus 5.5's $10.04 but above GPT-6 Astra's $6.25. Carbon's higher index score is therefore a capability result, not proof of the lowest total cost.

Arena supplies a different and useful signal. Carbon is preliminary number one in the Text Arena and number two in Agent Arena, behind Opus 5.5. Its Agent Arena result is based on real sessions and includes confirmed success, steerability, bash reliability, and tool hallucination signals. The early standing supports Carbon's broad promise, but the preliminary label and shorter collection window matter. Blind preference and agent-session outcomes should complement, not replace, task-specific acceptance tests.

sections.heading: Opus, Astra, and Argon remain the controls a buyer can deploy
paragraphs: Claude Opus 5.5 remains the strongest available control for difficult coding and judgment-heavy knowledge work. It leads the current Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index and the Agent Arena overall. Its $4/$20 token rate matches Carbon's standard price, making the eventual comparison unusually direct. Carbon uses fewer output tokens in the independent Intelligence Index run, while Opus leads coding agents and real-session agent outcomes. The winner will depend on whether a workload rewards scientific reasoning, terminal execution, polished deliverables, or consistent completion under tools.

GPT-6 Astra is the cost and engineering control at the premium end. Artificial Analysis places Carbon above Astra on the new general index, but Astra's measured $6.25 cost per Intelligence Index task is lower than Carbon's standard-price $7.76. Astra is already integrated into OpenAI's public API and has a mature migration path for teams using the Responses API. Carbon may justify switching on workloads where its higher reasoning result prevents retries; it does not justify switching merely because 59 is larger than another composite score.

Gemini 4 Argon is the practical Google choice today. It is generally available through the stable Gemini API, has documented 1M unified context behavior, and currently uses the same $2/$10 introductory rate. Carbon's independent gains make Argon a likely future predecessor, but Argon can be evaluated, integrated, and monitored now. Teams that need Google infrastructure should keep Argon in production and reserve a clean challenger slot for Carbon rather than designing around an unavailable model.

sections.heading: Wait for access, then run a narrow four-way evaluation
paragraphs: The smallest useful plan is to do nothing operational until Carbon receives documented general API access. Collect twenty to fifty completed tasks in the meantime, including difficult repository changes, scientific analysis, long multimodal inputs, tool failures, and professional deliverables that previously needed correction. Preserve the prompts, tools, acceptance checks, reviewer decisions, latency, token classes, retries, and billed cost so the same work can be replayed when Carbon becomes available.

Run Carbon high against the current production route, not against every frontier model. Use Opus 5.5 when judgment and polished knowledge work dominate, Astra for premium engineering agents, or Argon for an existing Gemini deployment. Compare accepted completion and reviewer time before benchmark scores. Test cache-heavy and long-context cases explicitly, because a 95% cache discount and a one-million-token window matter only when the application can reuse context without crossing operational limits or encouraging wasteful prompts.

Google reports state-of-the-art cybersecurity scores, more secure code, fewer unsupported claims, and better resistance to prompt injection. Those are vendor-reported launch results, even when the named benchmarks are public. Artificial Analysis's intelligence, coding, token-use, and task-cost findings are independent but still harness-specific; Arena's standings are independent but preliminary. The buying rule is therefore restrained: watch Carbon, keep a test slot ready, and switch only after public access and owned-task evidence turn an impressive model launch into a repeatable production advantage.
bullets: Wait: Carbon has no general API access or published rollout date.
Available Google route: Gemini 4 Argon at the same announced introductory token rate.
Capability control: Claude Opus 5.5; premium engineering control: GPT-6 Astra.
Vendor-reported: Google's cyber, safety, and internal coding gains; independently measured: Artificial Analysis and Arena results.
